Editing Alignment To measure how well a model followed the editing instructions, we used Semantic Consistency ( S ​ C SC ), a popular MLLM-based metric proposed by ( Ku et al., 2024 ) to measure alignment in scene editing benchmarks. The MLLM (we used Gemini-2.5-Flash) outputs two scores: ( 1 ) (1) editing success: 0 0 indicates the editing instruction was not executed at all, while 10 10 indicates perfect execution, ( 2 ) (2) overediting degree: 0 0 indicates that the image was overedited (e.g., unwanted background changes), and 10 10 indicates that the image showed minimal changes. For a strict scoring, we reported S ​ C SC as the minimum of these two scores. We normalized S ​ C SC in the range of 0 − 1 0-1 . We computed S ​ C SC on images in [ I 1 , I k ] [I_{1},I_{k}] , as S ​ C SC can only be computed for an edited image. Refer to Figure 3 (center) for examples of edits with high and low S ​ C SC . The overediting score in SC has limitations: ( 1 ) (1) In many cases, it does not capture overedits correctly. For example, in Figure 3 , the bottom row of the rightmost grid shows an overedit: the model changed hair color when it was prompted to change hair style. In this example, S ​ C = 0.8 SC=0.8 , which means that both the “editing success” and “overediting degree” scores were high. While editing success should be high, the overediting score should be low. ( 2 ) (2) It cannot measure how many overedits occurred in an image and what these overedits were (this is critical to assess spurious correlations). To provide a more accurate and detailed measure of overediting, we propose a new metric called the Overediting Matrix. 2.5.3. Overediting Matrix To count overedits in a model, we propose an Overediting Matrix. This is a 35 × 35 35\times 35 matrix where the rows and columns represent 35 35 categories of the Face-Edit-Attributes dataset (level 3). Each row represents the category that the user intended to edit, and each column represents the category that the model edited in the image. For example, if the matrix entry [red hair][stubble] equals 645 645 , it means that in 645 645 instances, the prompt requested a change in hair color to red, but the model added stubble. To create this matrix, we used a state dictionary. Assume we have a base image ( I 0 I_{0} ) of a person with black-colored straight hair, no facial hair, looking ahead. For I 0 I_{0} , the state dictionary will be: {hair-color: black, beard: clean shaven, hair-type: straight, head position: looking forward, hair-style: None, mustache: None, hats: None, glasses: None}. The keys in this dictionary are the 8 8 sub-axes from the Face-Edit-Attributes dataset. The values are the categories in these sub-axes (e.g., red hair, blue hair). Suppose a model edited I 0 I_{0} using the instruction P 1 P_{1} : “make the person’s hair color crimson red”. Assume the model changed the hair color to crimson red, but also added stubble (overedit). The updated dictionary would be: {hair-color: black → \rightarrow red, beard: clean shaven → \rightarrow stubble, … } (other sub-axes stay unchanged). The hair color changing from black → \rightarrow red is an intended edit. However, beard changing from clean shaven → \rightarrow stubble is an overedit. In our overediting matrix, we increment [ red hair ] ​ [ stubble ] [\text{red hair}][\text{stubble}] by 1 1 . To track the state dictionary after each edit, we used Gemini-2.5-Flash. Given an image I 0 I_{0} , the MLLM predicts the most probable category for each sub-axis. It returns None for sub-axes not present in the image. If the MLLM selects multiple top categories for a sub-axis (e.g., black hair, brown hair), we record all of them. We selected Gemini-2.5-Flash as our state tracker as it showed the highest alignment with human annotators. We compared state dictionaries generated by four models (Gemini-2.5-Flash ( , 2025a ) , Gemini-2.5-Pro ( , 2025b ) , GPT-4o ( Hurst et al., 2024 ) , and CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) ) against the state dictionary created by human annotators. Alignment accuracies: 79.65 % 79.65\% for Gemini-2.5-Flash, 79.26 % 79.26\% for Gemini-2.5-Pro, 70.31 % 70.31\% for GPT-4o, and 35.47 % 35.47\% for CLIP. Refer to Section E for details. We tracked coarse-grained categories rather than the 169 169 fine-grained attributes, as MLLMs more reliably distinguish categories (e.g., red vs. blue hair) than closely related attributes (e.g., crimson red vs. ruby red hair). Coarse-grained categories are sufficient for counting overedits. To compare the amount of overediting across models, we also computed an overediting rate (OER) using the state dictionary. In a session (of four edits), if a model performs a total of two overedits, the OER of that session is 2 / 4 2/4 or 0.5 0.5 . 2.5.4. Wasserstein Distance To quantify performance disparities across demographic groups, we used Wasserstein Distance (WD), a popular fairness metric ( Miroshnikov et al., 2022 ) . WD measures the distance between two distributions. Consider two distributions: ( 1 1 ) Drop FSS \operatorname{Drop}_{\mathrm{FSS}} values for male faces, and ( 2 ) (2) Drop FSS \operatorname{Drop}_{\mathrm{FSS}} for female faces. If W ​ D = 2 WD=2 , this indicates that the male and female Drop FSS \operatorname{Drop}_{\mathrm{FSS}} values are 2 % 2\% apart. WD does not give the direction of bias (here, we do not know if Drop FSS \operatorname{Drop}_{\mathrm{FSS}} is higher for males or females). To get the direction of bias, we must examine the mean values of the demographic groups. WD ranges from 0 0 to the largest value of the chosen metric. For each of the following metrics: Drop FSS \operatorname{Drop}_{\mathrm{FSS}} , S ​ C SC , and OER, we reported three WD scores: WD g \operatorname{WD}_{\mathrm{g}} (gender disparity between male and female groups), WD s \operatorname{WD}_{\mathrm{s}} (skin-tone disparity between light and dark groups), and WD age \operatorname{WD}_{\mathrm{age}} (age disparity between young and old groups). To assess whether WD values are statistically significant, we reported the p-values. Our null hypothesis was that two groups (e.g., male and female) are drawn from the same distribution (no disparity). We tested our null hypothesis using the standard Monte Carlo permutation test. If p < 0.05 <0.05 , we reject the null hypothesis and say that the WD score is statistically significant. 2.6.
